q: Which picture of particle motion in a liquid is correct?
o: Molecules stay in fixed places and only vibrate
Molecules fly freely far apart with no attractions
Molecules move randomly and slide past one another
Molecules are completely at rest unless heated
x: In a liquid, molecules are close together but keep moving randomly and slide past each other. Fixed vibrating positions describe solids; free, distant molecules describe gases.

q: Compared with the molecules of a gas, the molecules of a liquid are:
o: Much farther apart, with more empty space
Arranged in a fixed regular lattice
Much closer together, with little empty space between them
The same distance apart, but moving faster
x: Liquid molecules are packed closely with little free space. A gas is mostly empty space, and a regular lattice belongs to a crystalline solid.

q: A crystal of potassium permanganate placed at the bottom of a beaker of still water slowly colours all the water. This shows that liquid molecules:
o: Are held rigidly in fixed positions
Are in constant motion, so particles spread by diffusion
Repel the permanganate ions strongly
Have no attractions between them
x: Without stirring, the colour spreads only because the moving water molecules jostle the ions about, i.e. diffusion. Liquid molecules do attract one another.

q: A liquid expands on heating because its molecules:
o: Move faster and push one another slightly farther apart
Become larger in size
Increase in number
Lose their intermolecular attractions completely
x: Heating raises the kinetic energy of the molecules, so they move more vigorously and their average separation increases. The molecules themselves do not grow.

q: As most liquids are warmed, their density:
o: Increases, because the molecules move faster
Decreases, because the volume increases while the mass stays the same
Stays the same, because the mass does not change
Increases, because the volume decreases
x: Density = mass/volume. Warming makes most liquids expand, so the same mass occupies more volume and density falls. Water between 0 and 4 °C is the exception.

q: The boiling points of the halogens increase in the order F₂ < Cl₂ < Br₂ < I₂ because:
o: Dipole–dipole forces grow stronger down the group
Hydrogen bonding grows stronger down the group
The covalent bond inside each molecule becomes stronger
London dispersion forces grow stronger as molecular size and number of electrons increase
x: Halogen molecules are non-polar, so only London forces act; larger electron clouds are more polarisable. Boiling does not break the covalent bond inside the molecule.

q: Which liquid has dipole–dipole attractions between its molecules but NO hydrogen bonding?
o: Propanone (CH₃COCH₃)
Methanol (CH₃OH)
Hexane (C₆H₁₄)
Water (H₂O)
x: Propanone is polar (C=O) but has no H bonded to O, N or F, so its molecules attract by dipole–dipole forces only. Methanol and water hydrogen-bond; hexane is non-polar.

q: Which of these is NOT a property of liquids?
o: A definite shape of their own
A definite volume
The ability to flow
The ability to diffuse
x: Liquids have a definite volume, flow and diffuse, but take the shape of their container because their molecules can slide past one another.

q: The normal boiling point of a liquid is its boiling point at an external pressure of:
o: 1 atm (760 mm Hg)
0.5 atm (380 mm Hg)
2 atm (1520 mm Hg)
10 atm (7600 mm Hg)
x: Normal boiling point is measured at standard atmospheric pressure, 1 atm = 760 mm Hg. For water it is 100 °C.

q: Wet clothes dry faster when they are spread out than when folded because:
o: A larger surface area lets more molecules escape at the same time
Spreading raises the boiling point of water
Folding lowers the temperature of the water
Spreading increases the intermolecular forces in water
x: Evaporation happens from the surface, so a larger exposed surface lets more water molecules escape per second.

q: While a pure liquid is boiling at constant external pressure, its temperature:
o: Stays constant, as the heat supplied is used to overcome intermolecular forces
Keeps rising steadily until all the liquid has boiled
Falls, because the fastest molecules escape
Rises and falls repeatedly
x: During boiling, the heat supplied (latent heat of vaporisation) separates molecules against their attractions instead of raising the temperature.

q: At 100 °C, the vapour pressure of pure water is:
o: 100 mm Hg
380 mm Hg
760 mm Hg
1520 mm Hg
x: Water boils at 100 °C at 1 atm, and at the boiling point vapour pressure equals the external pressure, 760 mm Hg.

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes boiling from evaporation?
o: Boiling occurs only at the surface; evaporation occurs throughout the liquid
Evaporation needs a fixed temperature; boiling occurs at any temperature
Boiling cools the remaining liquid; evaporation does not
Boiling occurs throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature for a given pressure; evaporation occurs only at the surface
x: Evaporation is a surface process at any temperature. Boiling forms vapour bubbles throughout the liquid, and only at the temperature where vapour pressure equals the external pressure.

q: Water in an open dish evaporates faster on a windy day because the moving air:
o: Lowers the temperature of the water
Increases the intermolecular forces at the surface
Carries vapour molecules away, so fewer return to the liquid
Raises the external pressure on the water
x: Wind removes vapour from above the surface, so fewer molecules condense back and the net rate of evaporation rises.

q: A closed flask holds water and its vapour at equilibrium at 25 °C. More water at 25 °C is added, leaving some space above it. The vapour pressure:
o: Increases
Decreases
Becomes zero
Stays the same
x: Vapour pressure depends only on the nature of the liquid and the temperature, not on the amount of liquid present.

q: At 1 atm, diethyl ether boils at 35 °C, ethanol at 78 °C and water at 100 °C. At 25 °C, the order of their vapour pressures is:
o: Water > ethanol > ether
Ether > ethanol > water
Ethanol > ether > water
Ether > water > ethanol
x: A lower boiling point means weaker intermolecular forces and a higher vapour pressure at any given temperature, so ether > ethanol > water.

q: Which hydrogen halide shows hydrogen bonding between its molecules?
o: HCl
HBr
HI
HF
x: Hydrogen bonding needs H bonded to a small, highly electronegative atom (F, O or N). Among the halogens only fluorine qualifies.

q: Ammonia (NH₃) boils at a much higher temperature than phosphine (PH₃) because:
o: PH₃ molecules are lighter than NH₃ molecules
NH₃ molecules are linked by hydrogen bonds
PH₃ molecules are linked by hydrogen bonds
NH₃ has stronger London forces than PH₃
x: N is small and highly electronegative, so NH₃ molecules hydrogen-bond; P is not, so PH₃ has no hydrogen bonds. PH₃ (34) is actually heavier than NH₃ (17).

q: HCl (36.5 g mol⁻¹) has a larger molar mass than HF (20 g mol⁻¹), yet HF has the higher boiling point. The reason is that:
o: HF molecules are associated through hydrogen bonds
HCl molecules are linked by hydrogen bonds
HF has stronger London forces than HCl
The H–F covalent bond must break when HF boils
x: Hydrogen bonds hold HF molecules together, so extra energy is needed to separate them. HCl has only weaker dipole–dipole and London forces.

q: How many lone pairs on the nitrogen atom of an NH₃ molecule are available to accept hydrogen bonds?
x: N has five valence electrons: three are used in N–H bonds, leaving one lone pair. Oxygen in water has two.

q: Water needs a large amount of heat to change into vapour (a high enthalpy of vaporisation) mainly because:
o: Covalent O–H bonds must be broken
Water molecules are very heavy
Water has only weak London forces
Many hydrogen bonds between molecules must be broken
x: Vaporisation separates molecules, so the extensive hydrogen bonding between water molecules must be overcome. The O–H bonds inside each molecule stay intact.

q: A hydrogen bond is best described as:
o: A covalent bond shared between two molecules
A strong electrostatic dipole–dipole attraction
An ionic bond between H⁺ and an anion
A weak London dispersion force
x: The partly positive H on F, O or N is attracted electrostatically to a lone pair on a neighbouring electronegative atom; it is a strong kind of dipole–dipole force.

q: Hydrogen bonds between NH₃ molecules are weaker than those between H₂O molecules because:
o: Nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen
Nitrogen has more lone pairs than oxygen
NH₃ molecules are heavier than H₂O molecules
Nitrogen is more electronegative than oxygen
x: N (3.0) is less electronegative than O (3.5), so the N–H bond is less polar and its H carries a smaller partial positive charge. N has one lone pair, O has two.

q: Ice floats on liquid water because:
o: Ice is denser than liquid water
Ice contains air bubbles only
Ice has no hydrogen bonds
Ice is less dense than liquid water
x: Ice (about 0.92 g cm⁻³) is less dense than liquid water (about 1.00 g cm⁻³), so it floats. Its open hydrogen-bonded structure causes this.

q: The anomalous behaviour of water, such as its maximum density at 4 °C, is due to:
o: London dispersion forces
Ionic bonding
Hydrogen bonding
Metallic bonding
x: Hydrogen bonds arrange water molecules into an open structure in ice, which partly survives just above 0 °C; this gives water its unusual density changes.

q: The density of pure water at 4 °C is about:
o: 0.92 g cm⁻³
1.09 g cm⁻³
1.00 g cm⁻³
0.80 g cm⁻³
x: Water reaches its maximum density, about 1.00 g cm⁻³, at 4 °C. The value 0.92 g cm⁻³ belongs to ice.

q: When 1.00 dm³ of water (1.00 g cm⁻³) freezes, the ice formed (density 0.92 g cm⁻³) has a volume of about:
o: 0.92 dm³
1.09 dm³
1.00 dm³
0.80 dm³
x: Mass = 1000 g. Volume of ice = 1000/0.92 ≈ 1087 cm³ ≈ 1.09 dm³, i.e. water expands by about 9% on freezing.

q: An ice cube (density 0.92 g cm⁻³) floats in water (density 1.00 g cm⁻³). The fraction of its volume below the water surface is about:
x: A floating object sinks until it displaces its own mass of water, so fraction submerged = 0.92/1.00 = 92%. Only about 8% stays above the surface.

q: In autumn, as the surface water of a lake cools from 10 °C towards 4 °C, it:
o: Becomes less dense and stays at the surface
Freezes at once into a layer of ice
Stays at the same density and does not move
Becomes denser and sinks, so warmer water rises to the surface
x: Above 4 °C, water gets denser as it cools, so cold surface water sinks and warmer water rises, until the whole lake reaches about 4 °C.

q: For most substances the solid is denser than the liquid. Water is unusual because its solid form:
o: Has its molecules packed more closely than in the liquid
Has an open hydrogen-bonded structure with more empty space than the liquid
Contains no hydrogen bonds at all
Is made of ions instead of molecules
x: In ice, hydrogen bonds hold the molecules in an open arrangement with large spaces, so ice takes up more volume than the same mass of liquid water.
